description: Learning, adapting, applying, and solving problems.
summary:
Plant vs Climate is a free decision-support web tool that helps farmers and advisers compare crop rotations that protect soil, use water wisely and cope with a changing climate. It combines 20 years of NASA POWER climate data with NASA satellite evidence, optional soil information, crop characteristics from FAO tables, and each farmer's own priorities. It turns these into side-by-side comparisons of four rotation strategies (the current one plus three alternatives), with clear scores, charts, and the evidence, risks and information gaps behind each option.

Every score comes from transparent rules and NASA data, so each result can be traced back to its source. The user can fill in the setup by hand, or use an optional AI chat that fills in the form for them to confirm; the AI never calculates a score.

This answers the Field Shift challenge by turning NASA Earth observations into practical, location-level comparisons. Farmers face shifting temperatures, irregular rainfall, water shortages and declining soil health, and choices based on tradition alone may no longer fit those conditions. By making free NASA data usable for everyday farm decisions, Plant vs Climate aims to support long-term soil health and more efficient water use. It supports local expertise and does not replace it. Scores rank options; they are not yield or profit forecasts.
details:
What it does. Plant vs Climate is a decision-support tool for farmers, extension officers and advisers. The user first chooses a place: search by name (village, town, district), paste coordinates, use the device location, pick a demo site (Kedah, Cameron Highlands or Iowa), or click a NASA satellite map. Any point on Earth works, rounded to about 1 km. The user then picks a rotation style (three seasons a year, or one main crop a year over three years), enters their current three-crop rotation, ticks the crops they could grow, and sets four priorities from 0 to 5: save water, build soil health, earn income, avoid risk. They get four rotations side by side: their current one (the baseline), the best match for their priorities, a water-wise option and a soil-building option. Each card has an overall score out of 100, five sub-scores, and expandable evidence, benefits, risks and information gaps. A plain sentence says why the top option comes first.

How the scores work. The app fetches NASA POWER daily temperature, rainfall and root-zone soil wetness for 2005-2024 for the chosen point. For every crop, in every season of every past year, it scores temperature fit, cold and heat days, and rain plus stored soil moisture against the crop's water need. Water need comes from FAO-56 crop-coefficient curves and a temperature-based evapotranspiration equation. Rotations are then scored on climate fit, reliability (share of past years that worked, and the worst year), water demand, soil health and a rough relative income. An optional field elevation corrects POWER's temperature by 6.5 C per 1,000 m (checked at Cameron Highlands: 23.6 C raw became 18.1 C against about 17.9 C reported locally). Two what-if sliders shift temperature and rainfall to re-rank the options; this is a shift of the past record, not a forecast.

NASA satellite evidence (not scored). For Kedah and Iowa the app shows MODIS vegetation, evapotranspiration, surface temperature, leaf area and growing-season dates, and Landsat 30 m NDVI. NASADEM elevation and slope are shown for all three demo sites. For Kedah it also shows one year (2024) of SMAP soil moisture. A page section ("Where the NASA data goes") says which data drives the scores and which is evidence only. The satellite points were chosen so that they sit on cropland (MODIS pixels checked with MODIS land cover, Landsat pixels with ESA WorldCover); Cameron Highlands has no satellite pixel because its farms are too fragmented.

Long-lived crops. Tea, coffee, oil palm and banana stay in the ground for years, so they are not rotated and are not in the rotation scores. A separate card on the Climate page checks whether the place's average temperature suits them, today and with +1 to +4 C of warming, using FAO thermal-zone suitability ratings (S1 best to N not suitable). It covers temperature only (not rain, soil, frost, heat waves or disease) and says so on screen; it is a first filter, not a forecast of survival. Cocoa, rubber and olive are not included because the FAO table has no row for them.

How we checked it. Crop water needs, growing periods and temperature bands come from FAO tables. The water model was compared with MODIS potential evapotranspiration (ours ran 0.73 times MODIS in Kedah and 0.86-0.90 times in Iowa, correlation 0.94-0.98) and the gap is stated in the app. POWER rainfall was compared with NASA GPM IMERG for 2015-2024 (Kedah 2,417 mm against 2,464 mm a year; Iowa 821 mm against 990 mm, so Iowa scores are sensitive to the rainfall product). 274 automated tests pin sourced numbers to their published ranges and run the engine on real NASA POWER data.

Honest limits. Several crop values (cold and heat limits, tolerance ratings, market value, clover and cover-crop entries) are general agronomy knowledge, not sourced, and the app labels them. Soil rules other than FAO-56 water-holding are unverified judgement. Seasons are fixed at four months. There is no soil survey, market price, labour or equipment data. The rankings have not been validated against farm outcomes or tested with farmers.

Who it helps. Farmers, extension officers and advisers who want a quick, evidence-based first comparison before local expert advice. It is free, with no accounts, ads or tracking. A saved farm stays on the user's own device; place names typed into the search go to Open-Meteo, and chat text goes to Groq, only when those features are used. A "Get local advice" box points users to the Department of Agriculture Malaysia (doa.gov.my).

Reading and keeping the results. A plain-language sentence says why the top rotation comes first; any two rotations can be compared side by side; a year-by-year grid shows which of the 20 past years each crop suited the climate; results download as a spreadsheet (CSV); a farm can be saved on the device only and resumed; and an offline copy of the app and the three demo sites can be kept on the device (the offline rules are tested in code; not yet tried on a real phone without a connection).

Optional AI assistant (beta). Users who prefer to describe their farm in words can choose "Ask the AI" on the first page, after choosing the location. A model hosted by Groq asks a few questions and proposes setup values; the user checks and applies them. It never changes the location and never produces a score. If the AI service is off or busy, the manual setup works exactly the same.

Built with. React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet; hosted on Cloudflare Workers (static assets plus one small API route for the assistant). Apache-2.0 licensed. The slide deck and poster were made with PptxGenJS, react-icons (Feather icons) and node-qrcode, all MIT-licensed. Source code: https://github.com/HONGYANG-j/NASA-FIELD-APP . Full list of sources in References.

Links. Live app: https://crop-rotation-explorer.pahang-risk-nav.workers.dev . 30sec demo video, 3-5 minute project video, project document (PDF) and team poster: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1I8LMuO67uo7f15SnOTMdZhncomDgW7cv?usp=sharing
